headline: If Democrats win the House, the subpoenas start
summary: House Democrats are drawing up investigations of Trump, his family and his Cabinet in case they win the chamber in November. Hakeem Jeffries, in line to be speaker, says impeachment is neither ruled in nor out. Jamie Raskin, who would chair Judiciary, calls the list gargantuan. Democrats expect the White House to ignore subpoenas.

cover_question.q: Can they make the president answer?

cover_answer: They can order it. The White House may just not reply.
table_question: Who should get to check up on the person in charge?

5-7.script: In our country the people who make the laws also get to check on the president, like a hall monitor who can ask any teacher what they are doing. One team of lawmakers says that if they win the vote in November, they will start checking on the president and his family. That is how the country is built, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A hall monitor who can question a teacher. Checks on grown-ups are a thing they know.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script puts the rule in a person they can picture: a hall monitor who can question a teacher. It skips the party names and keeps the idea that someone checks on the president. Expect "is the president in trouble?" Not yet. Nobody has won the vote.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Congress can investigate the president: it is a separate branch that can demand papers and answers. But the majority picks what gets investigated. If Democrats win the House in November, they get the chairs and the subpoenas. Like a referee who finally gets the whistle.
8-12.why: Win the vote, get the chairs, send the subpoenas.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and who gets to enforce them, so the script hands them the chain: win the majority, get the chairs, send the subpoenas. The whistle only works in the referee's mouth. Expect "what if the president says no?" Democrats say they expect that. The article does not say who wins that fight.

13-17.script: Is a third impeachment worth anything if the Senate acquits again? Trump was impeached twice and acquitted twice, and Jeffries will not rule a third in or out. Second: Democrats say they expect the White House to ignore subpoenas. What is oversight worth if the other side will not answer?
13-17.why: Two open questions. Let them say which one bothers them.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: Congress has the power to investigate, and the White House may not answer. The script asks what the power is worth then, and whether a third impeachment is a tool or a gesture. Let them argue it first. Expect "is this justice or payback?" Raskin says the aim is corruption a law could fix.

5-7.q: Can they make the president answer?
5-7.a: They can order him to. The article says Democrats are getting ready for a White House that ignores the orders. Then the grown-ups argue about it.

8-12.a: A legal order to hand over papers or answer questions.
Letters go almost daily. But the majority signs the subpoenas.

13-17.q: Would they really impeach him again?
13-17.a: Jeffries won't rule it in or out. Cabinet members are the likelier targets.
Raskin says the aim is corruption a law could fix. Watch what they find.
